aluminiumAa8000.name: Aluminium conductor alloy, AA-8000 series (61.0 % IACS)

sources.citation: NBS Handbook 100, Copper Wire Tables (1966; https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/Legacy/hb/nbshandbook100.pdf, read in full by electrical-realism-reviewer), on the International Annealed Copper Standard (adopted by the IEC in 1913; 1925 is a revised edition): annealed copper at 20 °C (293.15 K) has a resistivity of 1/58 Ω·mm²/m (1.72414 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m, defining 100 % IACS), a temperature coefficient of resistance of 0.00393 per kelvin and a density of 8.89 g/cm³; resistance is treated as linear in temperature up to 200 °C (473.15 K), where the engine clamps R(T). Paraphrased; no table reproduced.

NBS Handbook 109, Aluminum Wire Tables (1972; https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/Legacy/hb/nbshandbook109.pdf, read in full by electrical-realism-reviewer), its first table at 61.0 % IACS: a resistivity of 0.028264 Ω·mm²/m (2.8264 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m) at 20 °C, a temperature coefficient of resistance of 0.00403 per kelvin at 20 °C and a density of 2.703 g/cm³. Aluminium building wire is an AA-8000-series alloy (ASTM B800, paywalled, not read); 61.0 % IACS is taken as the grade's assumed minimum conductivity, so this row is the 8000-series conductor at that conductivity. Al/Cu resistance ratio 1/0.610 = 1.6393. Paraphrased; no table reproduced.

game-design: the linear temperature-coefficient model is taken to hold for the aluminium alloy up to the same 200 °C (473.15 K) as copper. Handbook 109 gives α at 20 °C; its validity range for the 8000-series alloy was not verified.

Specific heat near 25 °C derived from the NIST-JANAF Thermochemical Tables (M. W. Chase Jr., 4th ed., J. Phys. Chem. Ref. Data Monograph 9, 1998) through the solid-phase Shomate fits published in the NIST Chemistry WebBook (read): copper 24.47 J/(mol·K) ÷ 63.546 g/mol = 385 J/(kg·K); aluminium 24.21 J/(mol·K) ÷ 26.982 g/mol = 897 J/(kg·K), the pure metal standing in for the dilute 8000-series alloy. Taken as constant over the conductor's temperature range (it rises slowly with temperature), an abstraction the thermal model states.

The International Temperature Scale of 1990 (H. Preston-Thomas, Metrologia 27, 3-10, 1990), whose defining fixed points include the freezing points of aluminium (933.473 K) and copper (1357.77 K). A public reference, not re-read for this table: electrical-realism-reviewer to confirm (ADR 0018 §5). Pure aluminium stands in for the 8000-series alloy, whose solidus is slightly lower. The engine burns a conductor or termination open when its node reaches the melting point, and never reports a node above it (F3.6 part 2).
